pull_quotes.after_paragraph: The popular idea of insider trading is almost right, but the law is narrower and stranger.
pull_quotes.quote: Insider trading is not about who you are: it is about what you know.
pull_quotes.rationale: Encapsulates the article's core insight in a memorable, quotable line.

sidebars.body_markdown: An insider who is permanently in possession of UPSI (e.g., a CFO) can still trade legally by adopting a pre-approved trading plan. The plan must be formulated in advance, disclosed to the stock exchanges, and executed automatically. Because the plan was set before the insider knew the UPSI, trades under it are not considered motivated by inside knowledge. This allows insiders to sell shares for legitimate reasons like tax planning without violating the law.
sidebars.rationale: Explains a key exception that readers might otherwise miss; sidebar keeps the main text focused.
sidebars.title: The trading plan safe harbour

tables.after_paragraph: The regulations give a non-exhaustive list of six categories that ordinarily qualify as UPSI
tables.footnote: Source: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, Schedule III.
tables.rationale: Concrete examples ground the abstract concept of UPSI; a table is more scannable than a list in prose.
rows: Quarterly profit or loss figures before the exchange filing
A surprise dividend announcement or a dividend cut
A bonus issue, stock split, or buyback
A takeover bid or a large order win outside normal business
The CFO resigning or being replaced
A rating upgrade or downgrade by a credit agency
tables.title: Categories of unpublished price-sensitive information
